summary: Defines a general way to locate an application service by domain name, without relying on rigid naming conventions known as name hacks. It uses SRV records and the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System to map a domain, service name, and protocol to a target server and port.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3958 defines a DNS-based way to find an application service using the domain, service, and protocol. The client follows a short chain of DNS records to reach a server and port, with alternatives if a target fails.

questions: how to find a service by domain name
how do naptr and srv records work together
what are the s and a flags in naptr
how does a client find a server using ddds
subtitle: Use DNS records to find a service by domain, service type, and protocol.

tldr.problem: An application needs to locate a service without relying on fixed host-name conventions, and a service may be hosted in another domain.
tldr.mechanism: S-NAPTR uses ordered NAPTR records to identify a service and protocol, then follows a replacement to more NAPTR records, SRV records, or address records.
tldr.outcome: Clients can follow ranked alternatives and retry another target when a lookup or connection fails. RFC 8553 later updates RFC 3958's underscored DNS naming rules.

today: RFC 3958 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. RFC 8553 updates its use of underscored DNS node names to align with the IANA registry.

sections.title: Finding Services Without Fixed Host Names
sections.content:
Applications often need to find the server that provides a service for a domain. A single SRV lookup can identify servers and ports, but does not support all the indirection needed when services are hosted by another organization.

RFC 3958 defines Straightforward-NAPTR (S-NAPTR), a restricted use of the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System. It uses both NAPTR and SRV records to map a domain, application service, and protocol to a target server and port.
sections.plainLanguage: A service name does not have to match a fixed server name. S-NAPTR lets domain owners point a client through DNS records to the service host.

sections.title: How S-NAPTR Resolution Works
sections.content:
The client retrieves NAPTR records for the target domain and sorts them by increasing ORDER, then PREF. It selects a record whose SERVICE field matches the requested application service and a protocol the client supports.

An empty flag means another NAPTR lookup follows. The terminal flag S leads to an SRV lookup; A leads to an address lookup. This application uses replacement targets, not NAPTR regular expressions.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sorts the domain's NAPTR records and chooses a matching service and protocol. The record's flag tells it whether to look for another NAPTR record, an SRV record, or an address.

sections.title: Retrying Targets in Preference Order
sections.content:
A domain can provide more than one target for a service and protocol. If a lookup yields no expected record, the connection fails, or the server lacks suitable credentials for the original domain, the client returns to the ordered list and tries the next matching path.

A client supporting several protocols completes the resolution and tries the targets for one protocol before moving to another. It must not switch protocols halfway through a resolution chain.
sections.plainLanguage: If one target cannot be used, the client can try the next matching target. It completes one protocol's resolution before trying another protocol.

sections.title: What the DNS Records Represent
sections.content:
Application service tags identify the kind of service, independently of the protocol used to provide it. Application protocol tags identify the protocol. The NAPTR SERVICE field combines these tags.

Only the S and A flags are terminal in this application. The replacement field identifies the next lookup target, and SRV records can then provide the host and port.
sections.plainLanguage: The service tag says what the client is looking for; the protocol tag says how it can connect. DNS records connect those choices to a host and port.

sections.title: Security Depends on DNS and the Application
sections.content:
If an attacker changes a NAPTR or SRV answer, the client can be redirected to an unintended destination. The RFC notes that DNSSEC can help validate DNS records.

Applications should also authenticate the server for the original domain during their own protocol handshake. S-NAPTR does not define that handshake or how credentials are matched to the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS records can be changed to point clients at the wrong server. DNSSEC and an application-level check of the server's identity address different parts of this risk.
